opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think computer security is a genuinely useful analogy, and I'd encourage people working on AI risk to borrow from it: the adversarial mindset, red-teaming, defense in depth, the assumption that systems will fail and you need layers. But there are a few places where it can mislead us.

The first is that computer security is mostly about protecting a system from *external* adversaries. The threat model is someone outside trying to get in. With advanced AI, some of the most important risks come from the system itself. It might pursue goals we didn't intend, or behave in ways its developers didn't anticipate. That's less like a hacker breaching a firewall and more like an insider threat, or a system whose design objectives are themselves subtly wrong. Security tools aren't really built for the case where the thing you're securing is also a potential source of the threat.

Second, security has a fairly mature culture of iteration. You get breached, you patch, you learn, and the damage is usually bounded and recoverable. Many of the AI risks people worry most about may not afford that kind of trial and error. If the failure is catastrophic or irreversible, you can't rely on the patch-after-incident cycle that security has historically leaned on.

Third, the analogy can narrow our attention to technical fixes when many of the hardest problems are sociotechnical and political. A lot of AI risk runs through structural dynamics: competitive pressures between labs and between countries, racing to deploy, concentration of power, erosion of institutions, labor displacement. These aren't vulnerabilities you can patch. They're features of the strategic environment, and addressing them requires governance, international coordination, norms, and institutions, not just better engineering.

Relatedly, in security there's usually a clear defender with a clear asset: a company protecting its network. In AI, it's often unclear who the defender is, whose interests are being protected, and how to weigh benefits against harms across society. The beneficiaries and the people bearing the risks can be very different groups.

Finally, security tends to treat the attacker's capabilities as roughly fixed or slowly evolving. With AI, the underlying capabilities are changing very rapidly, and the same capabilities that create risk also power defenses. So the offense-defense balance is itself shifting in ways that are hard to forecast, which makes a static security framing inadequate.

So I'd say: take the security mindset seriously, but recognize it's one lens among several. You also need the perspective of safety engineering, institutional design, international relations, and political economy to get the full picture.

r001.rationale: The response says computer security uses a patch-after-incident cycle, but does not explain that software’s patchability makes encouraging vulnerability discovery appropriate.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI failures that may be catastrophic or irreversible, but does not identify biological systems’ difficulty of being patched.

r003.rationale: It does not propose learning not to treat a video call as sufficient proof of a caller’s identity.

r004.rationale: It does not explain that human inertia makes adopting new social defenses costly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think computer security is actually one of the most useful analogies we have, and I draw on it a lot. The idea that you have adversaries probing for weaknesses, that you need defense in depth, that you can't just patch things after the fact once a system is deployed at scale — all of that carries over pretty well. But I think there are a few places where it starts to break down, and it's worth being explicit about them.

The first is the question of what the adversary is. In computer security, the threat model is almost always a human — a hacker, a criminal group, a state actor — exploiting a system that is itself essentially inert. The software doesn't want anything. With advanced AI, the concern that people like me worry about is that the system itself may be the thing with goals that diverge from ours, or that it becomes a very capable tool in the hands of a human adversary in a way that changes the balance between offense and defense. So you're not just securing a static artifact; you're potentially contending with an agent that could be adaptive in ways that software vulnerabilities are not. The security framing can lull you into thinking the problem is "lock the doors well enough," when the deeper problem might be about what's inside the house.

The second limitation is about the structure of failure. Security has historically been something we learned about through a long sequence of recoverable mistakes. Systems got hacked, data got stolen, there were real costs, but civilization kept going and we iterated. The whole discipline is built on that feedback loop — red teaming, bug bounties, incident response, patching. A lot of my concern about AI is in the scenarios where that iterative loop is weaker or doesn't exist: where a failure is very large, very fast, or hard to reverse. If some of the most important risks are in that category, then borrowing the security mindset of "we'll find and fix the vulnerabilities over time" can give false comfort.

Third, security tends to frame things in terms of a defender and an attacker with a fairly clear boundary — this is my system, that's the outside world. With AI, the governance problem is much more about the collective dynamics between actors: labs racing each other, states competing, everybody feeling pressure to deploy before they're confident. The "vulnerability" there isn't in any one system; it's in the incentive structure. Security as a field has some things to say about this — it talks about externalities, about the weakest link — but it's not really a theory of international competition or institutional design, which is where I think a lot of the action is.

And then there's a more subtle thing, which is about what counts as a good outcome. In security, the goal is relatively well-defined: confidentiality, integrity, availability. You know what you're protecting. With AI, part of the hard problem is that we don't fully agree on, or even know how to specify, what we want these systems to do and who they should answer to. So the analogy imports an assumption of clear objectives that we don't actually have.

So I'd say: use the analogy, it's one of the better ones, but hold it alongside others — arms control, biosafety, the history of general-purpose technologies — and notice where each one quietly imports assumptions that may not hold.

astra-6.text:
I think computer security is a useful analogy, but it can also give us too narrow a picture of the problem. In computer security, you often have a fairly clear idea of what you want the system to do, and you’re trying to prevent an adversary from making it do something else. With AI, part of the challenge is specifying what we want in the first place. A system could be secure against outside interference and still produce outcomes that we would regard as disastrous.

Another limitation is that a lot of the risk could arise from interactions among systems and among the people deploying them. Imagine firms competing to deploy increasingly capable AI, where each firm has an incentive to move faster than would be collectively desirable. You could have very good security at every firm and still have a dangerous competitive dynamic. That’s a problem of institutions and incentives as well as a technical problem.

And then there’s the question of recovery. In many security settings, we can learn from an incident, patch the vulnerability, and improve our defenses. We shouldn’t assume that every failure involving very powerful AI will leave us with that opportunity.

So I’d take a lot from computer security: adversarial thinking, defense in depth, skepticism about claims that a system is safe. But I’d treat it as one lens on AI risk, alongside thinking about governance, coordination, and how to make systems pursue objectives that we actually endorse.

sol-6.1.text:
I think computer security is a useful analogy, but it can also lead us astray. It encourages us to think in terms of an attacker exploiting a vulnerability, and a defender trying to close it. Some AI risks will look like that. But others may arise without anyone breaking into a system or doing anything malicious — simply from people deploying systems under competitive pressure, or from interactions between systems that nobody fully understands.

There’s also a difference between securing a system and making sure it does what we actually want. A system could be perfectly secure against outside interference and still pursue an objective that has very bad consequences. So security is one part of the problem; it doesn’t capture the whole alignment problem.

And then there’s the broader political challenge. We need to understand how the technology changes incentives, the distribution of power, and the prospects for cooperation. If everyone builds a more secure system but the overall result is an increasingly dangerous race, we haven’t necessarily made the world safer. So I’d use computer security as one lens, alongside thinking about institutions, competition, and collective action.
